turns.en: Welcome to Longview. I'm Ben Johnson, Head of Client Solutions with Morningstar. And I'm Amy Arnott, Portfolio Strategist for Morningstar. Today's guest on the Longview is Robin Wigglesworth.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 The Long View。我是 Ben Johnson，晨星（Morningstar）客户解决方案主管。我是 Amy Arnott，晨星的投资组合策略师。本期 The Long View 的嘉宾是 Robin Wigglesworth。

turns.en: Robin is the editor of the Financial Times finance blog, AlfaVille. He's also the author of Trillions, which is the definitive book on the past, present, and future of passive investing.
turns.zh: Robin 是《金融时报》（Financial Times）财经博客 Alphaville 的编辑，也是《Trillions》一书的作者——那本书堪称关于被动投资过去、现在与未来的权威之作。

turns.en: Robin's joining us today to discuss his latest book, A Fabulous Debt, which is a history of the bond market. Amy, there's an old adage that says, don't judge a book by its cover.
turns.zh: Robin 今天加入我们，聊聊他最新的著作《A Fabulous Debt》，这是一部债券市场史。Amy，有句老话说：不要以貌取书。

turns.en: And I think that applies probably as much to A Fabulous Debt as any other book. I think it face value a lot of our audience might think, oh goodness, a book about the history of bond markets, how boring could that possibly be?
turns.zh: 我觉得这话放在《A Fabulous Debt》这本书上再合适不过了。就表面看，我们很多听众大概会想：天哪，一本讲债券市场历史的书，能有多无聊啊？

turns.en: And I think what we've discovered in our conversation with Robin is that it's anything but the history of the bond market is marked by war, peace, market mania, features a very colorful cast of characters and so much more.
turns.zh: 但在我们与 Robin 的对话里我们发现，它一点也不无聊。债券市场史充满了战争、和平、市场狂热，还有一大帮色彩斑斓的人物，远不止于此。

turns.en: So I was really fascinated to hear Robin share the history of bonds with us today. Yeah. That's a great point. And Robin is such a brilliant writer that he really brings every aspect of a history to life.
turns.zh: 所以我特别期待今天听 Robin 为我们讲述债券的历史。是啊，说得太对了。Robin 是个非常出色的写作者，他把历史的每一个侧面都写得栩栩如生。

turns.en: And for me, one of the highlights was when he was talking about the huge amount of capital spending we're seeing in AI and how it kind of parallels the railroad boom in the 19th century.
turns.zh: 对我来说，其中一个亮点，是他讲到我们在 AI 上看到的巨额资本开支，以及它如何与 19 世纪的铁路热潮遥相呼应。

turns.en: He made the point that debt-fueled capital spending sprees tend to end quite badly, although the scale of capital investment in AI, this time around, is still quite a bit smaller.
turns.zh: 他提到，靠债务驱动的资本开支狂潮往往以相当糟糕的方式收场，只不过这一次 AI 的资本投资规模还是要小得多。

turns.en: It was a really interesting point and history rarely repeats, but often rhymes and we might be living through one of those rhyming moments today.
turns.zh: 这一点特别有意思——历史很少重演，但常常押韵，而我们今天或许正身处某个押韵的时刻。

turns.en: So without further ado, let's dig in with Robin. Robin, welcome to the Longview. Thank you so much for joining Amy and I. Thanks for having me on, Amy and Ben.
turns.zh: 那就不多说了，我们来请出 Robin。Robin，欢迎登上 The Long View。非常感谢你加入，陪我和 Amy 聊一聊。谢谢邀请我来，Amy、Ben。

turns.en: I've been looking forward to this. Robin, we're really excited to dig into this just expansive exploration that you're publishing here, looking into the origins and the evolution of the bond market.
turns.zh: 我一直很期待这次对谈。Robin，我们非常兴奋能深入聊聊你在这本书里展开的这场恢弘探索——追溯债券市场的起源与演进。

turns.en: But I want to start by asking you about the origin story of the book itself. In the introduction, you share a quote from American novelist Toni Morrison who said that, and I quote, if there's a book you want to read but it hasn't been written yet, then you must write it, end quote.
turns.zh: 不过我想先从这本书本身的起源故事问起。你在引言里引用了美国小说家 Toni Morrison 的一句话，我念一下：如果有一本你想读的书却还没被写出来，那你就得自己去写它。

turns.en: So my question is, was your motivation in writing this book entirely self-serving? This is just a book that you'd always wanted to read, but no one had yet written.
turns.zh: 所以我的问题是：你写这本书的动机完全是出于自己的喜好吗？这只是一本你一直想读、却还没人写过的书？

turns.en: Well, I'm no Toni Morrison, obviously, but yes, it is highly self-serving. This is a book that I wanted to read myself. Fixing Come Bonds, it was my first love as a financial journalist.
turns.zh: 我当然算不上 Toni Morrison，但没错，这确实很大程度上是为自己而写。这是我自己想读的一本书。固定收益（fixed income）债券，是我做财经记者时的初恋。

turns.en: My first job out of university was writing about Islamic bonds, of all things. Sukuk, they're called, and I just thought it was fascinating, both Sukuk but Fixing Come in general.
turns.zh: 我大学毕业后的第一份工作，就是写伊斯兰债券（Islamic bonds）——也就是 Sukuk（苏库克），说什么都算冷门。我当时就着迷了，无论是 Sukuk 还是整个固定收益市场。

turns.en: I just think it's just exhilarating, and it's almost like the hidden wiring of the global economy. I'm not saying everything makes perfect sense when you understand the bond market or capital markets, but at least more things are less mystifying, essentially.
turns.zh: 我觉得它令人兴奋，几乎是全球经济的隐形布线。我不敢说理解了债券市场或资本市场，一切就都说得通了，但至少很多事不再那么神秘莫测了。

turns.en: So I would always read a lot about the bond market. I'd read lots of books about Mike Milkin or Louis Ranieri, a bit of Alexander Hamilton. But then in 2018-19, I was playing around with the BIS database, as all cool people do like to do on a Saturday night.
turns.zh: 所以我一直读了很多关于债券市场的东西。我读过很多关于 Michael Milken、Louis Ranieri 的书，也读过一些关于 Alexander Hamilton 的内容。但到了 2018、2019 年，我在摆弄国际清算银行（BIS）的数据库——所有酷的人周六晚上都爱干这事。

turns.en: And I realized there, from their date at least, that the bond market was not just bigger than the stock market, that's been the case for a very long time, but it actually is bigger than the banking system.
turns.zh: 然后我发现，至少从他们给出的数据来看，债券市场不仅比股票市场大——这一点长期以来都是如此——它实际上比整个银行体系还大。

turns.en: And for me, that was electrifying, because I think there are so many things that flow from that, essentially, that the entire financial system is ordered around the idea that banks are the central engine.
turns.zh: 对我来说那非常震撼，因为由此引出的东西太多了。整个金融体系都是围绕“银行是核心引擎”这个观念来组织的。

turns.en: And really now, when you look at some credit and debt, it's less than half the total. In fact, lots of bank assets are, of course, in the form of bonds.
turns.zh: 而如今你要是看看信贷和债务，银行占的比重还不到一半。事实上，银行资产里很大一部分本身就是以债券的形式存在。

turns.en: So then I had the sense that this is an important story, and then I realized, actually, I had over the years read so many things about bonds and bond market history that maybe I could try and stitch it all together into one coherent, compelling narrative, so that people realized the enormous sense of how bonds have shaped the world we live in in so many ways that, I think, people don't really appreciate, but is particularly true in the US.
turns.zh: 于是我感觉这是一个重要的故事。然后我意识到，多年来我读了太多关于债券和债券市场历史的东西，也许我可以把它们缝合起来，串成一个连贯、迷人的叙事，让人们真正体会到债券在多少方面塑造了我们生活的世界——而这些往往不被人重视，在美国尤其如此。

turns.en: So you shared that Ian Fleming actually chose the surname Bond for James Bond, because he thought it was the dullest name he'd ever heard. But you also write that the bond market has often proven just as prone to fits of delusional mania and periodic disasters as a stock market.
turns.zh: 你提到 Ian Fleming 之所以给 James Bond 选了“Bond”这个姓，是因为他觉得这是他听过的最乏味的名字。但你也写道，债券市场同样经常沉迷于妄想的狂热和周期性灾难，一点也不输给股票市场。

turns.en: Why do you think people often still think of bonds as a boring but necessary part of finance? Well, there are probably two components to that.
turns.zh: 你为什么觉得人们至今仍把债券看作金融中“无聊但必要”的一部分？嗯，我想大概有两层原因。

turns.en: One is that bonds ideally should be boring. Most of the time, they are designed to be boring, even if they have quite often been anything but.
turns.zh: 其一，债券最好就该是无聊的。大多数时候，它们的设计初衷就是无聊，尽管它们常常一点也不无聊。

turns.en: We want the bond market to be boring, because when the bond market is exciting, it's usually not a great time. And then the other thing, the aspect, is just complexity.
turns.zh: 我们希望债券市场无聊，因为当债券市场让人兴奋的时候，通常都不是什么好时候。另一层原因就是复杂。

turns.en: Even quite a lot of people in the finance industry, my impression actually is think the bond market is a little bit annoying. And bond yields can go up and down for good and bad reasons.
turns.zh: 我印象里，甚至在金融行业内都有不少人觉得债券市场有点烦人。债券收益率会因为好原因或坏原因上下波动。

turns.en: It doesn't always feel as intuitive as the stock going up, for example. And therefore, it's quite easy to relegate to the nerds of the financial system.
turns.zh: 它不像股价上涨那样直观，因此人们很容易把它推给金融体系里那些书呆子。

turns.en: I think that's massively wrong. I think the bond market is fascinating in its own right, but also massively important. But I do think ever since 2008, there's been a great appreciation in the equity world that the bond market is really the one.
turns.zh: 我觉得这大错特错。我认为债券市场本身就极迷人，同时也极其重要。不过我确实认为，2008 年以后，股票世界越来越体会到，债券市场才是真正的主宰。

turns.en: To use a lot of the rings metaphor is the one ring that rules us all. The equity market, it's important, it's dramatic, it's glamorous, it's fun.
turns.zh: 借用一句魔戒的比喻，它就是那“一枚戒指，统领全部”。股票市场重要、戏剧化、光鲜、有意思。

turns.en: I love stock market world as well, but if I had to choose one thing to write about for the rest of my life, it'd be the bond market every day of the week.
turns.zh: 我也爱股票市场的世界，但如果一辈子只能选一个题材来写，我天天都选债券市场。

turns.en: Robin, as much as bonds are the main character of the book, it seems like inevitably you introduced this whole sort of cast of supporting characters spending some time talking about the intersection of fixed income in equity markets, the development of global central banks, currencies and currency rates fixed and pegged.
turns.zh: Robin，尽管债券是这本书的主角，但我觉得你不可避免地引出了一整帮配角——花了不少篇幅讲固定收益与股票市场的交汇、全球央行的发展、汇率与货币的固定和盯住。

turns.en: Gold shows up. Did you fully appreciate when you set out to write the story of bonds that you would have such an expansive cast of supporting characters that you would have to provide treatment to as well?
turns.zh: 黄金也出场了。当初动笔写债券这个故事时，你有没有充分意识到，你会带出这么一大帮需要分墨去描写的配角？

turns.en: I'd say yes, but that was the biggest pitfall I was wary of because on one hand I did want to tell a broader story than just bonds. Bonds are the hero, my protagonist, but I wanted to tell a more expansive story about high finance and the economy has evolved and to help people understand where we are today and what the future might look like.
turns.zh: 我会说是，但那正是我最警惕的陷阱。一方面，我确实想讲一个比债券更宏大的故事。债券是主角、是我的主人公，但我想讲一个关于高端金融和经济如何演进的更恢弘的故事，帮助人们理解我们今天所处的位置，以及未来可能的样子。

turns.en: I think history is fascinating and important in its own right, but really what makes it compelling is because it is vital for us to understand what's going on today.
turns.zh: 我觉得历史本身既迷人又重要，但真正让它引人入胜的，是它对理解当下至关重要。

turns.en: So I wanted to tell that broader story, but I also was very wary of going down the rabbit hole side quest essentially on the parallel evolution of banking and money and central banking and all sorts of other aspects because really you could use the bond market to tell just a 20 volume story of the history of global finance.
turns.zh: 所以我想讲那个更宏大的故事，但我也非常警惕别一头扎进支线——关于银行、货币、央行以及种种其他方面的平行演进。说真的，光用债券市场就能讲出一部二十卷的全球金融史。

turns.en: I didn't want to go too far down those rabbit holes except when I felt it was really essential. So there is obviously a fair bit of central banking there, especially towards the end.
turns.zh: 我不想在这些支线里走得太深，除非我觉得实在必要。所以书里当然有不少关于央行的内容，尤其是后半部分。

turns.en: You can't not talk about money because one of the original selling points of bonds actually was that it was a little bit like fancy money back in an era where there was obviously no electronic money and there was quite often a shortage of species.
turns.zh: 你不能不谈货币，因为债券最初的一个卖点，其实就像是一种高级货币——在那个既没有电子货币、又常常金银短缺的年代。

turns.en: So Alexander Hamilton, he used bonds as sort of a, I think in the musical, Lin-Manuel Miranda called it a financial diuretic for the revolution-wracked economy, but I think that's kind of, it was essential to the story I want to tell.
turns.zh: Alexander Hamilton 就把债券当作一种……我想在那部音乐剧里，Lin-Manuel Miranda 称之为给战乱经济的“金融利尿剂”。我觉得这确实是我想讲的故事里不可或缺的部分。

turns.en: But I had to, in journalism terms, there's this expression called kill your darlings, that we all have these things that we fall in love with, little turns of phrase or sections or themes that we love, but might actually not be essential and in fact are distracting to the reader.
turns.zh: 但用新闻行业的说法，有个词叫“杀死你的挚爱”（kill your darlings）。我们都有些自己钟爱的东西——某个漂亮的措辞、某段文字、某个主题——但它们未必真正必要，反而可能让读者分心。

turns.en: And I had to murder just an insane number of my darlings when I was writing this book, but hopefully I'll have material for a second or third or fifth or tenth edition at some point.
turns.zh: 写这本书时，我不得不“谋杀”掉多得惊人的挚爱，但希望将来某一天还能攒出第二版、第三版、第五版、第十版的素材。

turns.en: So if we go all the way back to the birth and early development of the bond and bond markets, you use a metaphor of a horse and carriage where you write that the Venetians were the first to invent the wheel, but it was the Dutch who realized that if you put four wheels together, that made it a more useful wagon.
turns.zh: 如果我们一路回到债券和债券市场的诞生与早期发展——你用了一个“马车”的比喻。你写道，威尼斯人最先发明了轮子，但荷兰人意识到把四个轮子凑到一起，就变成一辆更有用的大车。

turns.en: And then later on, the British tethered horses to this wagon and charged ahead. So if we go all the way back to the beginning in 12th century Venice, why was that particularly time and place so conducive to the birth of bonds?
turns.zh: 后来英国人又给这辆大车套上骏马，一路狂奔。那我们回到起点，12 世纪的威尼斯——为什么那个时间和地方如此适宜债券的诞生？

turns.en: Well, there had been sort of things that kind of walked or quacked like bonds before the Mesopotamians traded clay tablets of loans that Romans invented in UTIs.
turns.zh: 嗯，在那之前也有过一些像债券、或者“走得像、叫得像债券”的东西。美索不达米亚人交易过刻在泥板上的贷款，罗马人则发明了欠条（IOU）。

turns.en: But I think this first prestige it was called in Venice is really the granddaddy because you can see a very clear intellectual lineage from that bond in Venice to the other Italian city-states.
turns.zh: 但我觉得威尼斯的“prestiti”（预借款）才是真正的老祖宗，因为你能看到一条清晰的血脉传承：从威尼斯的这笔债，到其他意大利城邦。

turns.en: They spread across Europe and were iterated by the Dutch, the British, the Americans and so on. But you can see a very clear sort of lineage as a family tree there.
turns.zh: 它们传遍欧洲，又被荷兰人、英国人、美国人一路迭代。你能看到一幅非常清晰的家族谱系图。

turns.en: Venice is just unique and fascinating and I mean, obviously one of the favorite things about writing book is all the research you get to do.
turns.zh: 威尼斯独一无二，又迷人。说到写书最让人享受的一点，就是你能名正言顺地做那么多研究。

turns.en: And Venice, I knew the abstract story that was a very commercial, important town in the Middle Ages and visited Venice. It's beautiful. Have either of you been there?
turns.zh: 威尼斯，我原本只知道一个抽象的故事——它是中世纪一个非常重要、商业气息浓厚的城镇，也去过威尼斯，那里很美。你们二位谁去过吗？

turns.en: I've not. I haven't. No. Well, it's crawling with tourists, which is maybe unavoidable when it's so beautiful, but it is an incredible unique city and it was unique at the time.
turns.zh: 我没去过。我也没去过。没。嗯，那儿满是游客，美得如此大概也难免，但它是一座不可思议、独一无二的城市，在当时就已经独树一帜了。

turns.en: It was founded by immigrants and refugees basically fleeing the vandals, literally the vandals. And they settled in this swampy armpit of Italy because nobody else wanted to live there.
turns.zh: 它是由移民和难民建立的——基本上是在逃离汪达尔人（the Vandals），字面意义上的汪达尔人。他们就在意大利这片沼泽旮旯里安了家，因为没别人愿意住。

turns.en: And they built the town precariously on stilts hammered into the swamp lands. So it's largely almost like a floating city. And they had no real nobility.
turns.zh: 他们把城市摇摇欲坠地架在打进沼泽的木桩上，所以它几乎就是一座漂浮之城。他们没有真正意义上的贵族。

turns.en: They weren't rich in natural resources, there's salt and fish, that's about it. But they're genius. And I still don't understand exactly how it happened, how this occurs, and magically there was commerce.
turns.zh: 他们自然资源也不丰富，就是盐和鱼，仅此而已。但他们聪明绝顶。我到现在也没完全想明白这一切是怎么发生的——商路就那么神奇地出现了。

turns.en: They owed their fealty as Catholics to the Pope in Rome. Their suzerain at the time was actually the Byzantine emperor in Constantinople, today's Istanbul.
turns.zh: 他们作为天主教徒要向罗马教皇效忠，而当时的宗主其实是君士坦丁堡（今伊斯坦布尔）的拜占庭皇帝。

turns.en: But they essentially, their only loyalty was to trade. They would trade with absolutely everybody, the Ottomans, the Mamluks, everybody they would trade with.
turns.zh: 但本质上，他们唯一的忠诚是给贸易的。他们和所有人做生意——奥斯曼人、马穆鲁克人，来者不拒。

turns.en: And that annoyed everybody. And I think it was almost inevitable that a city state of such relentless, enormous wealth, ingenuity, commercial drive was where the first bond was going to be born, even if it was just frankly an accident, how it actually came about.
turns.zh: 这让所有人都恼火。我觉得，一座如此不知疲倦、如此巨富、如此聪明、商业驱动力如此之强的城邦，注定会孕育出第一笔债券——尽管它实际的诞生方式坦白说纯属偶然。

turns.en: Well, I've never been to Venice, I've been to another famous city known for its canals in Amsterdam. And I think one of the first branches of this bond family tree was born out of the sort of Dutch iteration of the Venetian invention to borrow from your metaphor.
turns.zh: 我虽然没去过威尼斯，但去过另一座以运河闻名的城市——阿姆斯特丹。我想，债券家族谱系的第一个分支，就是从荷兰人对威尼斯发明的那次迭代里长出来的——借用你的比喻。

turns.en: The Dutch realized that having not just one wheel, but putting four wheels together made for a stronger wagon. So how specifically did the Dutch parlay that Venetian invention of the bond to use it ultimately as the basis for what became the Dutch golden age?
turns.zh: 荷兰人意识到，不止一个轮子，把四个轮子凑一起会造出更结实的大车。那么，荷兰人具体是如何把威尼斯发明债券这一招，运用成他们“黄金时代”的根基的？

turns.en: Well, so the Venetians invented the bond by accident, like I said, because it was actually a war tax that they raised more proportioning from all the citizens to pay for a war against Constantinople.
turns.zh: 嗯，威尼斯人是阴差阳错发明了债券，就像我说的，那其实是战争税——他们向全体市民按比例征收更多税款，用来支付一场对君士坦丁堡的战争。

turns.en: And they made the receipts for this tax tradable. And it was a war loan, essentially, that they had to pay. And because they lost that war, that war loan, temporary war loan became permanent, but it paid 5% interest and you could trade the receipts.
turns.zh: 他们让这笔税的收据可以交易。那本质上是一笔战争贷款，他们必须偿还。因为他们打了败仗，这笔临时战争贷款就变成了永久的，但它支付 5% 的利息，而你可以交易这些收据。

turns.en: So that ended up being quite a valuable thing. And the Venetians, you know, they built on this. They decided this was a valuable thing. People could use it as collateral for trade, but they never really kind of embraced the full potential as much as the Dutch.
turns.zh: 于是这东西最终变得很有价值。威尼斯人在此基础上又加了码，他们意识到这东西有用——人们可以拿它做贸易的抵押品——但他们始终没能像荷兰人那样充分释放它的潜力。

turns.en: In Venice for a long time, only Venetians were allowed to buy the city's own bonds, basically the Pristiti, the Monti mountain, as it was eventually called.
turns.zh: 在威尼斯，有很长一段时间只有威尼斯人被允许购买本城自己的债券——基本上就是那些 presti，后来被称作 Monti（意为“山”，即公债基金）。

turns.en: Because the Dutch made it a real market, a vibrant market where lots of other people were. Dutch towns, provinces, water utilities, and actually companies.
turns.zh: 是荷兰人把它做成了一个真正的市场——一个充满活力的市场，很多人参与其中：荷兰的城镇、行省、水务部门，甚至公司。

turns.en: The Dutch East India Company, the first global conglomerate, pioneered the stock market as well. It was the first listed company, but it also pioneered corporate bonds.
turns.zh: 荷兰东印度公司——第一家全球性集团——也开创了股票市场，它是第一家上市公司，同时还是公司债券的先驱。

turns.en: So you suddenly see people really embracing the power of bonds to essentially pool vast amounts of small sums into one big, titanic sum, essentially.
turns.zh: 于是你突然看到人们真正开始运用债券的力量，把无数小额资金汇成一大笔、一笔巨额的资本。

turns.en: And I think that was incredible and no coincidence that the Dutch had kind of taken over the Venetian crown as the most mercantile, most ambitious, most commercially minded people in Europe at the time.
turns.zh: 我觉得这太了不起了，而且绝非巧合——荷兰人那时已经取代威尼斯人，成了欧洲最善经商、最有野心、最具商业头脑的民族。

turns.en: And lo, they then took the bond and really started to show off to other Europeans the power of it. And it had existed in Germany as well around then.
turns.zh: 就这样，他们接过债券，开始向其他欧洲人展示它的威力。债券当时在德国一带也存在。

turns.en: It spread from Italy to the Germanic states, into France, where they're called Rants and Edenten in Germany. But the Dutch were the ones that used it first to keep the country dry.
turns.zh: 它从意大利传到日耳曼诸邦，传到法国——在法国叫 rentes，在德国叫 Renten。但荷兰人是第一个用它来让国土保持干燥的民族。

turns.en: I mean, a large part of the levelness is below sea level. So all the dites, the waterways that you see still to this day, almost all of them were paid for by the sale of bonds, by the local waterworks.
turns.zh: 我是说，荷兰很大一部分在海平面以下。你今天看到的几乎所有堤坝、水道，当初几乎都是靠地方水务部门发行债券筹建的。

turns.en: And they used that ability to pay for their own financing, raise financing, lots of financing, to fight a war of independence against Spain, which was the hyperpower of Europe at the time.
turns.zh: 他们利用这种自筹资金、大量融资的能力，去打一场反抗西班牙的独立战争——而西班牙正是当时欧洲的超级强国。

turns.en: So it was an 80-year war. It took a long time. It was a fantastically or horrifically destructive war, but they finally won independence. And it was because they could finance themselves almost to infinity and pay for, frankly, a lot of German mercenaries, a lot to fight for them as well, whilst the Spanish crown went bankrupt, I think in those 80 years, three or four times out of six times, and often
turns.zh: 那是一场八十年的战争，打了很久，是一场极其惨烈、破坏性极强的战争。但他们最终赢得了独立，靠的就是几乎能无限地为自己融资，去支付——坦白说——大批德国雇佣兵来为他们作战；而西班牙王室在这八十年里，好像六次破产中破产了三四次，

turns.en: couldn't pay its soldiers, there were bank strikes, and basically it was financially stricken. And the Dutch showed that if you take paying your debts quite seriously and nurture a vibrant bond market, then that can be an immense asset at times of crisis and war.
turns.zh: 常常发不出军饷，出现过军队哗变，基本上被财政拖垮了。荷兰人证明：如果你认真对待偿债、并培育一个充满活力的债券市场，那在危机与战争年代可以是一笔无比宝贵的资产。

turns.en: So if we fast forward to 1694, you have the establishment of the Bank of England, which was kind of the first step in Britain playing a major role in the evolution of global bond markets.
turns.zh: 那我们快进到 1694 年，英格兰银行（Bank of England）成立，这算是英国在全球债券市场演进中扮演重要角色的第一步。

turns.en: What were the major contributions that Britain made with respect to bonds? Yes. I mean, Isaac Newton lived around then. He always said that if I've seen further, it is because I stand on the shoulders of giants.
turns.zh: 英国在债券方面做出了哪些主要贡献？是的。我是说，Isaac Newton 就生活在那个年代。他常说，如果说我看得更远，那是因为我站在巨人的肩膀上。

turns.en: And I think one of the genius bits of British people, at least, they just unashamedly copy great ideas from other countries and take their best people for a long time as well.
turns.zh: 我觉得英国人至少有一点很聪明——他们毫不脸红地从别的国家照搬好点子，还长期把别国最优秀的人才挖为己用。

turns.en: And the English had fallen, frankly, behind the Dutch around this time. And they rather cheekily just basically imported the Dutch prince, William of Orange, to be their new king.
turns.zh: 在那段时间前后，英格兰坦白说已经落后于荷兰了。于是他们相当大胆地把荷兰的亲王——奥兰治的 William——请来当自己的新国王。

turns.en: It was a bit of a protestant because the current king was Catholic and there was all sorts of controversy around that. But really, alongside a Dutch prince, they also imported and almost copied and pasted lots of Dutch inventions when it came to money and financing.
turns.zh: 那有点像一场新教徒的政变，因为当时的国王是天主教徒，围绕这事引发了种种争议。但关键是，除了请来一位荷兰亲王，他们几乎把荷兰人在货币与融资上的诸多发明照搬照抄了过来。

turns.en: And they set up a central bank that was partially modeled on the Vistal Bank in Amsterdam. But one of the most impactful things that they did was, and there was no one single person that kind of said, this is what we're going to do.
turns.zh: 他们建立了一家央行，部分参照了阿姆斯特丹的 Wisselbank（汇兑银行）。但他们做过的影响最深远的举措之一——而且并没有某一个人拍板说“我们要这么干”，

turns.en: It happened almost gradually over many people doing it. But essentially, the Dutch were a collection of provinces and states and towns. And they had this very vibrant bond market.
turns.zh: 它是在许多人身上逐渐发生的。本质上，荷兰是一个由行省、邦国和城镇组成的集合体，它们有非常活跃的债券市场，

turns.en: But there was no real, even though there was a country called the Netherlands then, the Netherlands didn't really issue that much bonds. And in other parts of Europe, quite a lot of the people that sold bonds or borrowed money were the royal families.
turns.zh: 但尽管当时有个叫“尼德兰”的国家，尼德兰本身却并没发行多少债券。而在欧洲其他地方，发债或借钱的人很多是王室家族。

turns.en: That the king, usually a king, was synonymous with the kingdom. So the UK obviously had shown that wasn't the case. And Parliament was taking more and more control.
turns.zh: 国王——通常是国王——就等同于王国本身。英国已经证明这并非如此，议会的权力越来越大。

turns.en: So they made bond issuance, the responsibility and prerogative of Parliament, of the First Minister almost, although they hadn't started calling the Prime Minister yet, but of Parliament.
turns.zh: 于是他们把债券发行变成议会、几乎也就是首相的职责与特权——尽管那时还没开始叫“首相”——总之是归议会。

turns.en: And it made those bonds the explicit obligation of the United Kingdom, even before the United Kingdom was called that. And that was revolutionary because then suddenly you had an actual, proper, clear, cohesive, geographically identifiable nation-state that was issuing sovereign bonds.
turns.zh: 它让这些债券成为这个国家的明确债务——尽管那时“联合王国”还没这么称呼。这是革命性的，因为突然之间，一个真正的、规范的、清晰的、凝聚的、地理可辨的民族国家开始发行主权债券。

turns.en: And essentially, I mean, I still think that the Venetians issued the first sovereign bonds, even though there was just a city-state, but you can very easily time it with the establishment of the Bank of England.
turns.zh: 本质上，我还是认为威尼斯人发行了最早的主权债券，尽管那只是一座城邦。但你完全可以把它和英格兰银行的成立对应起来看。

turns.en: The Bank of England was set up to buy a big, fat UK government bond, which only got, it was a perpetual bond, as they used to be back then. But it was only paid back, I think, 10, 20 years ago symbolically, been outstanding for several hundred years until then.
turns.zh: 英格兰银行的设立，就是为了认购一笔庞大的英国政府债券——那是一种永续债（perpetual bond），在当时很常见。它直到大约一二十年前才被象征性地还清，此前已流通了好几百年。

turns.en: And that eventually morphed into what was called the console market. And the console market generally was a wonder of the age of reformation and the ages that came afterwards, because it was essentially the first huge homogenous stock of debt that was broadly traded and accepted around the world.
turns.zh: 那笔债最终演变成所谓的统一公债（consols）市场。统一公债市场堪称那个时代及此后时代的奇迹，因为它本质上是被全球广泛交易和接受的第一大同质化债务存量。

turns.en: The first true risk-free asset was the console market. And those console bonds cropped up everywhere, including among Britain's enemies in many wars.
turns.zh: 第一个真正的无风险资产，就是统一公债市场。这些 consols 债券随处可见，甚至在许多战争中出现在英国的敌人手里。

turns.en: French investors loved buying console bonds. Even during the Napoleonic War, they would quite often do so when they were on opposite sides because they liked that they were the obligation of a sovereign nation-state.
turns.zh: 法国投资者特别爱买 consols。即便在拿破仑战争期间，双方兵戎相见时，他们往往也照买不误——因为他们喜欢它代表着一个主权民族国家的债务。

turns.en: They liked the fact that the British had started opening the books. They'd actually start to be a little bit transparent about the government finances.
turns.zh: 他们喜欢英国人开始“打开账本”，也就是对政府财政开始有一点透明度。

turns.en: The Venetians had actually done so as well. But the Brits kind of show that this is a liability of the taxpayer as well. Ergo, the taxable, should be able to see some of the state finances.
turns.zh: 威尼斯人其实也这样做过，但英国人展示了这同时也是纳税人的责任——因此纳税人理应能看到一部分国家财政。

turns.en: And that gave investors confidence. And that's why you could see that as the first true risk-free asset, essentially, was the console market.
turns.zh: 这给了投资者信心。也正因如此，你可以说第一个真正的无风险资产，本质上就是统一公债市场。

turns.en: Robin, reading the book, it struck me that if the title had not already been taken long ago, that maybe war and peace would have been a decent title for a book about the history of the bond market.
turns.zh: Robin，读这本书的时候我忽然想到，如果这个书名没有被很久以前占用，《战争与和平》或许很适合做一本债券市场史的书名。

turns.en: And I think one of the examples where that is particularly apparent is just around sort of the birth and the infancy of the United States. Alexander Hamilton, who you referenced earlier, said that public debt was effectively a national blessing.
turns.zh: 我觉得最能体现这一点的例子之一，就发生在美国的诞生与襁褓期。你之前提到的 Alexander Hamilton 说过，公共债务实际上是一国之福。

turns.en: Yes. I'm just curious, what is the framing of that remark and what role did the sort of early evolution of the bond market in the United States play in both the war and the peace end of the equation?
turns.zh: 是的。我只是好奇，这句话的语境是什么，而美国早期债券市场的演进，在“战争与和平”这一主题里扮演了怎样的角色？

turns.en: I think no country on earth has been so profoundly shaped and aided by the bond market as the United States of America. I don't think actually most people, even in finance, appreciate what an incredible degree that is true.
turns.zh: 我觉得，地球上没有一个国家像美利坚合众国那样，被债券市场如此深刻地塑造和相助。我认为，其实即使是在金融圈，绝大多数人也不明白这在多大程度上是千真万确的。

turns.en: Alexander Hamilton, I found, or I found, I mean, Journal found them also long before me, of course, but Alexander Hamilton, when he was a young artillery captain, was obsessed with financial affairs.
turns.zh: 我发现——当然，很多记者比我早得多就发现了——Alexander Hamilton 年轻时当炮兵连长，就对财政事务极为着迷。

turns.en: He would read and study all the time that these letters he sent around to people talking about how the British console market, rather than being a public curse, this big national stock of permanent debt, it was actually one of Britain's greatest sources of strength because you could always issue more bonds because as long as you were credible, you always have willing buyers, even if you have to sometimes pay more to get that to entice
turns.zh: 他一刻不停地研读、给各方写信，论述英国的统一公债市场如何并非一种公共诅咒——那笔庞大的、永久的国家债务存量——反而是英国最伟大的力量源泉之一，因为你总能发行更多债券：只要你可信，总会有愿意接盘的买家，哪怕有时得多付一点利息去吸引他们。

turns.en: them. So that bond market became this kind of financial diuretic, as the musical called it. It could be used as collateral in trade. It could be used as something that kind of walk, talk, and crack like money in an era where actual coin was in desperate shortage of.
turns.zh: 于是债券市场成了那种“金融利尿剂”——正如那部音乐剧所说。它可以被用作贸易抵押品，可以在真金白银极度短缺的年代，扮演那种“看起来、听起来、走起来都像钱”的东西。

turns.en: So when he became the America's first Treasury Secretary, he put that plan into action. I think that was incredibly important for essentially getting the post-revolutionary economy of America going.
turns.zh: 所以当他就任美国第一任财政部长时，他把这套计划付诸实施。我认为，这对启动革命后的美国经济极其重要。

turns.en: But I think the other thing that is as important is that, and I haven't found any specific reference to the Venetians about this, but one thing that we saw in Venice was that by issuing debt or selling debt to your own citizens, you're creating citizen creditors.
turns.zh: 但我觉得同样重要的还有一点——我在威尼斯人那里还没找到具体的佐证——我们在威尼斯看到的一个现象是：通过向本国公民发行债务、卖债给本国公民，你就创造了一批“公民债权人”。

turns.en: It gives those citizens a vested interest in the country staying together, or the city in case of Venice, staying together, and gives them a vested interest in good governance as well.
turns.zh: 这让这些公民有了一份切身利害关系，希望国家——在威尼斯就是这座城——不要散，也让他们有了一份关心良政的切身利益。

turns.en: And basically by taking all those state debts that had been issued to fight the war, state by state, and turning them into federal obligations.
turns.zh: 基本上，就是把各州为打赢战争而各自发行的一大堆州债，转化为联邦的义务。

turns.en: So this was the assumption that was super controversial at the time, because the North generally was entirely bankrupt, and the South had slavery and plantations, and was generally able to pay back their debts after the revolution.
turns.zh: 这就是“承担州债”（assumption）方案，在当时极具争议，因为北方当时几乎完全破产，而南方有奴隶制和种植园，革命后大体上还能还清自己的债。

turns.en: By turning all these debts into a federal stock of debt, it gave all American citizens that were creditors also a vested interest in this very new nascent federal government surviving, which we now take for granted because we always think of histories A, then B, then C, then D. But in reality, these things aren't preordained, and history could have turned that very differently if essentially all these merchants and shopkeepers and nascent industrialists
turns.zh: 通过把全部这些债务变成联邦债务存量，每一位身为债权人的美国公民，都对这新生的、还很稚嫩的联邦政府能否存续有了切身利益。我们如今对此习以为常，总以为历史是 A、然后 B、然后 C、然后 D 这样顺下来的，但其实这些事并非命中注定。如果遍布各地的商人、店主和初生的实业家们对联邦政府能否维系没有那份切身利益，历史完全可能走向截然不同的方向——

turns.en: around America didn't have a vested interest in the federal government sticking together. The country could have been torn apart by all these centrifugal forces that were around at the time that did almost tear it apart later on.
turns.zh: 那时种种离心力量几乎可以把这个国家撕裂，而后来也确实差点把它撕裂。

turns.en: And so I just think that's an incredibly interesting, people focus a lot on Alexander Hamilton founding the first bank of the United States and all the other, I mean he was a man of just incredible intellectualism and energy, but I do think that his decisions around the assumptions of state debts was by far the most important and transformative decision almost taken by the federal US government at its birth.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这特别有意思。人们关注很多 Hamilton 创建了第一家美国银行之类的事——他当然是一个才思与精力惊人的人——但我确实认为，他在承担州债问题上的决策，几乎是美国联邦政府诞生之初所做过的最重要、最具变革性的决定。

turns.en: So one of the chapters in the book is called From Poitiers With Love, I hope I'm pronouncing that correctly. So this was billed as kind of a verdant territory in what is now Honduras.
turns.zh: 书里有一章叫《From Poitiers With Love》，希望我没念错。这一章讲的是如今洪都拉斯境内一片被吹得天花乱坠的“沃土”。

turns.en: What does that episode tell us about investor psychology? Yes, I mean this is, you know, I don't like to choose my favorite chapters or stories because it's a bit like choosing your favorite child, but you know, this is my favorite bit.
turns.zh: 这件事告诉我们关于投资者心理的什么？嗯，我是说，我不喜欢挑自己最喜欢的章节或故事，那有点像挑最爱的孩子——但这一段确实是我的心头好。

turns.en: It's just incredible. So there was a Scottish mercenary called Gregor McGregor, he's the distant descent of Rob Roy McGregor is a famous folk hero in Scotland.
turns.zh: 它太不可思议了。有个叫 Gregor MacGregor 的苏格兰雇佣兵，他是 Rob Roy MacGregor 的远亲——Rob Roy 是苏格兰有名的民间英雄。

turns.en: He fought in the Napoleonic Wars, couldn't settle down, then fought in all these revolutionary wars in Latin America. He fought with Simon Bolivar in the liberation of Venezuela from Spain and had all sorts of random escapades and adventures until he finally met the prince of a chunk of what is today Honduras and was gifted a piece of land that was verdant and rich and had the mahogany trees and gold nuggets running in the river, a huge gold mine that the locals
turns.zh: 他打过拿破仑战争，安分不下来，又去打拉丁美洲那一连串革命战争。他和 Simón Bolívar 一起把委内瑞拉从西班牙手中解放出来，经历了一堆离奇的冒险，直到最后遇到了今天洪都拉斯境内一片地方的亲王，对方赠给他一块肥美富饶的土地——有桃花心木林，河里流淌着金块，还有一座巨大的金矿，

turns.en: just didn't care about, but they'd be quite happy to work in for free, as he told people. And he was appointed the Kazik, the prince of this almost semi-independent country.
turns.zh: 只是当地人根本不上心——不过按他说的，他们倒是很乐意免费去干活。他被任命为这片半独立国度的 cacique（首领）。

turns.en: And he went to London in 1821, suddenly turned up, called Sir Gregor McGregor, the Kazik of Poyer. He wore highland dress all the time, he liked, you know, looking the part.
turns.zh: 1821 年他跑到伦敦，突然冒了出来，自称“Sir Gregor MacGregor，Poyais 的 cacique”。他一直穿苏格兰高地礼服，喜欢做足了派头。

turns.en: He was the toast of town, he met the royals. He went to all the fancy clubs. He had sung, sung, written and sung about this incredible land called Poyer.
turns.zh: 他成了伦敦社交界的宠儿，会见了王室成员，出入各种高级俱乐部，还有人为这片他口中的奇妙之地 Poyais 写歌、唱歌。

turns.en: He issued bonds, he compelled them, tried to sell land to encourage them, wanted to colonize and essentially bring Western know-how and carpentry and industrialism to this country.
turns.zh: 他发行债券，试图卖地吸引买家，想要殖民此地，把西方的知识、木工技艺和工业化带进这个国度。

turns.en: And he sold it as this land of milk and honey and gold nuggets. He even sold bonds on the London sockets chain, traising £200,000, which wasn't huge, but definitely, you know, it was a lot more money then than it is now.
turns.zh: 他把这片土地吹成流奶与蜜、遍地金块之地。他甚至跑到伦敦证券交易所（London Stock Exchange）上发债券，筹得 20 万英镑——数目不算巨大，但在那个年代绝对比现在值钱得多。

turns.en: And you know, several hundred families uprooted their lives to move to this incredible country. And then they landed and discovered it was a swampy hellhole and there was nothing, there was no capital, there was no gold, the natives didn't want them.
turns.zh: 有好几百户人家举家背井离乡，搬到这片“不可思议的国度”。结果他们登岸后发现，那是一处沼泽地狱，什么都没有：没有资本，没有黄金，当地人也不欢迎他们。

turns.en: And they, most of them, you know, some tragically committed suicide because some of the mental breakdown of landing there was just so bad. Many others died from dysentery, from famine, from disease.
turns.zh: 他们当中，有些人可悲地自杀了，因为登岸后的精神崩溃实在太过严重。更多的人死于痢疾、饥荒和疾病。

turns.en: And I think only sort of 20, 30 people made it back to the UK alive. And you know, Greg McGregor, outrageously, I mean, he took the money and spent it on all this huge fortune, but he kept insisting, no, no, this is real.
turns.zh: 我想只有二三十人活着回到了英国。而 Gregor MacGregor 厚颜无耻——他拿走了那笔钱，挥霍成一大笔财富，却仍不断坚持说：不，不，这是真的。

turns.en: And he sold another bond and he eventually had to escape to France and try to basically do the same scam there. But it's one of the most incredible stories, you know, it's basically a con artist.
turns.zh: 他又卖了一笔债券，最终不得不逃到法国，试图在那里故技重施。但这是最不可思议的故事之一——本质上他就是个骗子。

turns.en: I mean, we don't really know whether he might have just been a complete and utter fantasist. That was kind of one of the most outrageous examples of fake it to make it.
turns.zh: 我们其实不知道，他会不会完全就是个彻头彻尾的空想家。那是“先装成功，直到真成功”（fake it till you make it）最早、最离谱的范例之一。

turns.en: That maybe he hoped to genuinely fake it until he made a country. But it's incredible, but it shows that, you know, people in the bond market can also lose their minds.
turns.zh: 也许他是真的想一路“装”下去、直到真造出一个国家来。它不可思议，但也说明——债券市场里的人一样会丧失理智。

turns.en: And this was after the South Sea bubbles, we weren't that many stocks to speculate on. Bonds after the Napoleonic War became like the hot, cruel new thing to speculate on because everybody who had made, basically had invested in British consoles in the Napoleonic Wars, made out like bandits.
turns.zh: 那是在南海泡沫（South Sea bubble）之后，可投机的股票没那么多。拿破仑战争之后，债券成了投机客追捧的火热新宠儿，因为几乎所有在拿破仑战争期间买过英国 consols 的人都赚得盆满钵满。

turns.en: They made tons of money. So they wanted to invest in new bonds. So they invested first in Prussia and then in France and then they invest in the Spanish bonds and Russian bonds.
turns.zh: 他们赚翻了，于是想投新的债券。他们先投普鲁士，然后是法国，接着是西班牙债券和俄罗斯债券。

turns.en: And eventually you have these, all these newly independent countries, it's kind of like venture capital, but for fixed income through investing in these grand new ventures, Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil, and including Poyer.
turns.zh: 最后就轮到了所有这些新独立的国家——这有点像风险投资（venture capital），但投的是固定收益：投给这些宏大的新事业——委内瑞拉、哥伦比亚、巴西，也包括 Poyais。

turns.en: And Poyer is kind of the ultimate example of how much people lost their minds and what was one of the first big global financial crises that really emanated purely from finance, from financial speculation.
turns.zh: Poyais 可以说是人们如何集体失去理智的极致范例，它也是最早几场真正纯粹由金融、由金融投机引发的大型全球金融危机之一。

turns.en: The beans in the South Sea bubble that did ripple outside the UK, but this one, they say, true global crisis and caused, you know, banks to go bust in both London and the U.S.
turns.zh: 南海泡沫那波余波确实溢出英国之外，但这一场被称作真正波及全球，它导致伦敦和美国的银行纷纷倒闭，

turns.en: in Europe, almost all of Latin America defaulted on their debts. And it just goes to show, you know, bonds can be incredibly powerful when we treat them a bit like money.
turns.zh: 在欧洲，拉丁美洲几乎所有国家都违约了。它说明，当我们把债券当钱一样对待时，债券可以极其强大。

turns.en: But they're not always money. It's certainly not if you lend money to a country called Poyer or Argentina. But people in the 18, this is in the 1820s, they treated these bonds as like money so you could use them collateral for other loans.
turns.zh: 但它并不总是钱——你借给一个叫 Poyais 或者叫阿根廷的国家，那就更不是了。但在 1820 年代，人们把这些债券当成钱，可以拿去做其他贷款的抵押品。

turns.en: And then eventually when, you know, it all broke bad, it broke bad in a cataclysmic way. So it's just, I love that story because obviously it's just such an incredible scam.
turns.zh: 到最后，一切以灾难性的方式崩盘。所以我特别爱这个故事，因为它显然就是一场不可思议的骗局。

turns.en: And Gregor McGregor is just, I mean, a hilarious character. I mean, it's terrible to laugh at it now because people died, but, you know, the joke goes, the only difference between tragedy and comedy is time.
turns.zh: Gregor MacGregor 真是个让人忍俊不禁的人物。当然，现在拿它开玩笑有点不妥，因为死了人——不过有句玩笑话说：悲剧和喜剧之间，唯一的差别就是时间。

turns.en: So hopefully it's okay for us to laugh at Poyer now. And it just shows, yeah, I mean, the bond market can do all sorts of dumb things as well, even though it has this self-image, this self-regard as the serious market compared to the silly stock market, it's actually.
turns.zh: 所以希望我们现在拿 Poyais 开个玩笑还不算过分。它只是说明：债券市场也会干种种蠢事，尽管它自视甚高，把自己看成那个相对于“傻乎乎”的股票市场而言的“严肃市场”。

turns.en: So yeah, that's worth remembering even today. As a financial advisor, you've got your clients back and we've got yours. With Vanguard's actively managed bond funds, you're backed by consistent performance with a low cost edge for an advantage that keeps compounding and compounding and compounding.
