turns.en: And compounding and compounding and compounding. Are you backed by institutional quality bond funds? Vanguard. So Robin, I think Gregor McGregor and Poyer, an interesting example of at least attempting to fake it till you make it.
turns.zh: Robin，我觉得 Gregor MacGregor 和 Poyais 是个有趣的例子——至少是“尝试先装成功，直到真成功”。

turns.en: We've seen other investment cycles over the years where there wasn't necessarily any faking taking place, but maybe the till you make it bit didn't arrive quite as quickly as many expected.
turns.zh: 这些年我们见过别的投资周期，那里未必有什么“装”的成分，但“直到真成功”那部分没有像很多人预期的那么快到来。

turns.en: I'm curious when you look at that historical set of examples, do you think of railroad capex in the United States as being a prominent example?
turns.zh: 我很好奇，当你回望历史上这一系列例子时，你会不会把美国的铁路资本开支（capex）看作一个突出的例子？

turns.en: What are some of the common patterns there that you've seen play out over time? And do any of those in your mind rhyme with what we're seeing today in the market?
turns.zh: 你看到的那些反复出现的共同模式是什么？在你心中，它们当中有没有哪个和我们今天在股市上看到的情形押韵？

turns.en: I think most notably with the capex cycle we're living through in all things related to artificial intelligence. Yes. I mean, it's an excellent question and definitely one that is top of mind for a lot of people, including me right now.
turns.zh: 我想最明显的，就是眼下我们经历的这轮与人工智能（artificial intelligence）相关的资本开支周期。是的，这真是个好问题，也是此刻包括我在内很多人脑子里挥之不去的问题。

turns.en: I think one thing I saw repeatedly when I was studying 1,000 years of bond market history is that debt is an incredibly powerful tool, but we do misuse it like we misuse all our most powerful tools.
turns.zh: 我觉得在研究一千年债券市场史时，我反复看到的一点是：债务是一种威力极大的工具，但我们像滥用所有强大工具一样滥用它。

turns.en: And the bond market, maybe because it's like a technology that fundamentally allows you to borrow more money more cheaply, that essentially if you know you can sell a bond, the bond's supposed to be tradable, it's designed to be tradable, even if sometimes it isn't.
turns.zh: 债券市场——也许因为它本质上是一种让你能更便宜地借到更多钱的技术——只要你知道自己能发债、而债券理应是可以交易的、它的设计初衷就是可交易，尽管有时并非如此。

turns.en: If you're more likely to buy it, ergo, you generally pay a lower interest rate by selling a tradable security versus just going to a bank and hitting it up.
turns.zh: 于是你更可能买到，因此一般来说，出售一种可交易证券的利率，会比你直接去找一家银行张口借钱要低。

turns.en: And you can borrow it from thousands of people, but it's a technology that allows you to borrow more cheaply and to a greater degree. And that doesn't take a genius to see how that can lead to trouble.
turns.zh: 你可以向成千上万人借钱——这是一种让你借得更便宜、借得更多的技术。不用太聪明也能看出这会惹麻烦。

turns.en: But it can also, sometimes we do need to go a little bit nuts and build stuff. And that's when the stock market just isn't really, and the banking system isn't really enough to kind of conjure up those titanic sums.
turns.zh: 但它有时候也确实需要我们稍微疯狂一点、去建设一些东西。那种时候，股票市场和银行体系其实不足以变出那些天文数字的资本。

turns.en: Like generally speaking, all great human endeavors require a ton of money, whether they be wars or railways or now maybe artificial intelligence.
turns.zh: 通常来说，一切伟大的人类事业都需要海量资金，无论战争、铁路，还是如今的人工智能。

turns.en: So the railways is a great example because, you know, it's a way that the bonds kind of almost metaphorically help knit together the colonies into the United States of America and the same late 1700s, railways that were mainly financed by bonds in the US helped knit together the country physically.
turns.zh: 铁路是个很好的例子，因为债券几乎以一种比喻的方式，帮助把各个殖民地缝合成美利坚合众国；而 18 世纪末之后，主要靠债券融资的铁路，帮助把这个国家在物理上缝合到了一起。

turns.en: I write in the Fabulous there that the railways is like the physical skeleton of America. It really transformed the United States into the world's superpower, long before, frankly, people really recognized it inside the country and outside.
turns.zh: 我在《A Fabulous Debt》里写道，铁路就像美国的“物理骨架”，它真正把这个国家变成了世界超级大国——这远早于国内和国外的人们真正意识到这一点。

turns.en: But Americans, I mean, humans in general always get overly excited. And Americans, I do hope you'll forgive me for saying, are particularly good at getting overly excited by new technologies and financial booms.
turns.zh: 但美国人——我是说人类整体——总是过度兴奋。而美国人，请原谅我这么说，尤其擅长被新技术和金融热潮冲昏头脑。

turns.en: And so it proved with railways, it was, you know, I mean, there were actually many railway bubbles and bursts, but there was one particular massive one.
turns.zh: 铁路也是如此。其实出现过很多次铁路泡沫与崩盘，但其中有一次特别巨大的。

turns.en: And why it was so destructive was because it wasn't really equity driven. It was driven by debt, by bonds, massive amounts of bond sales, just, I mean, today, staggering sums.
turns.zh: 它之所以破坏性那么强，是因为它并非股票驱动，而是债务、债券驱动——天文数字的债券发行，坦白说，放到今天看也是惊人的规模。

turns.en: I mean, I want to do the calculations. If you look at the size of the US economy then and now, it'd be the equivalent of selling around what $10 trillion worth of bonds.
turns.zh: 我想好好算一算。如果你看看当时和现在的美国经济规模，那相当于发行了大约 10 万亿美元的债券。

turns.en: So, you know, the AI boom is still pathetic in comparison to the railway bubble. And it led to a cataclysmic crash in 1873, when America's leading bank, Jay Cook and Co, suddenly went under, brought under by his exposure to transcontinental railways, the northern Pacific line specifically.
turns.zh: 所以，跟铁路泡沫相比，眼下的 AI 热潮还显得“可怜”。它导致了 1873 年一场灾难性的崩盘——当时美国首屈一指的银行 Jay Cooke 公司（Jay Cooke and Co）突然倒闭，压垮它的是对跨大陆铁路、尤其是北太平洋铁路（Northern Pacific）的敞口。

turns.en: And I don't think today we can understand how big a shock that was, frankly, to the global financial system at the time. This was the equivalent of J.P. Morgan, suddenly saying, by the way, we're bankrupt.
turns.zh: 我觉得今天我们无法理解，那场冲击对当时全球金融体系究竟有多大。这就相当于 J.P. Morgan 突然来一句：顺便说一句，我们破产了。

turns.en: It ushered in what was long called the Great Depression. We now just call it the Long Depression, because the Great Depression was deeper. But the Long Depression that came after 1873 is still the longest in American history.
turns.zh: 它带来了很长时期里被称为“大萧条”（Great Depression）的那场危机；我们现在把它叫“长萧条”（Long Depression），因为后来那场“大萧条”更深重。但 1873 年之后的这场“长萧条”，至今仍是美国历史上最漫长的一次。

turns.en: It was exacerbated by all sorts of silly things afterwards, and obviously the US didn't have a central bank, so it couldn't manage the economic cycle so well.
turns.zh: 之后又有种种蠢事把它加剧了，而且美国当时没有央行，所以没法很好地调控经济周期。

turns.en: But it was a very bad crisis. I don't think we're there with AI yet, but there are so many interesting parallels in that kind of revolutionary technology, and we think of railways.
turns.zh: 但那是非常糟糕的一场危机。我不认为 AI 现在就到了那一步，但在“革命性技术”这一点上有很多有趣的平行之处——我们想想铁路。

turns.en: It's kind of hard for us to think of railways as revolutionary, because it's so everyday. It's kind of so 19th century, essentially. But railways were a stunning achievement at the time.
turns.zh: 我们很难把铁路想成什么革命性的东西，因为它如今太日常了，本质上太“19 世纪”了。但在当时，铁路是一项惊人的成就。

turns.en: We all genuinely thought that the human body wasn't made for such crazy speeds as 30 miles an hour. They thought you'd go mad by driving on railways.
turns.zh: 我们那时真的以为人体承受不了每小时 30 英里这种疯狂速度，以为坐火车会让人发疯。

turns.en: You thought that your brain might vaporize if you cross 40 miles per hour, and no country really embraced it more than the US. In Europe, railways went from one town to the next and connected existing towns.
turns.zh: 以为一旦超过每小时 40 英里你的脑子就会汽化。没有哪个国家比美国更狂热地拥抱铁路。在欧洲，铁路是从一座城镇连到下一座城镇，连接起已有的城镇。

turns.en: In the US, railways created towns, created states, Bismarck, capital North Dakota, isn't it? That's his name. That's a marketing gimmick. Bismarck to help market bonds by the Northern Pacific Railway to German investors, because Bismarck, Rotevon Bismarck was a child's world, Germany at the time.
turns.zh: 在美国，铁路创造了城镇，创造了州。Bismarck——北达科他州的首府，对吧？那是用俾斯麦（Bismarck）的名字——那是个营销噱头。北太平洋铁路用 Bismarck 这个名字，是为了向德国投资人营销债券，因为俾斯麦——Otto von Bismarck——在当时是德国万众瞩目的人物。

turns.en: Railways was just far bigger than AI is now, maybe in a few years' time, AI will rival it in size. On one hand, I'm more relaxed about AI than I am railways, because most of it's issued by very wealthy, long-established, financially strong companies like Metta and Alphabet and so on.
turns.zh: 铁路的体量远比今天的 AI 大，也许几年后 AI 的规模能与之匹敌。一方面，我对 AI 比对铁路更放心，因为它大多由非常富有、根基深厚、财务稳健的公司发行——像 Meta、Alphabet 等等。

turns.en: One thing that gives me a slight pause is that there's a fair bit of financial engineering going on, a lot of off-boundsheet liabilities that aren't visible to investors.
turns.zh: 让我略感迟疑的一点是：眼下有相当多的金融工程在运作，很多表外负债（off-balance-sheet）不为投资者所见。

turns.en: The fact that railways, a railway can go bust, the company can go bust, but the track, the blade is still there, and generally lasts for a very, very long time.
turns.zh: 还有，铁路公司可以倒闭，但铁轨、路基还在，通常会存在非常非常久。

turns.en: I don't think the same can be said for AI data centers with tips that seem to have to be replaced every few years. Maybe we'll come out of this with a few humble tech giants and cheaper compute for everybody for all our AI needs, but I do slightly worry that as this debt part of the cycle expends faster and faster, that the economic hangover is going to be that much worse, because it's debt-fueled capex sprees tend to end quite badly.
turns.zh: 我不认为 AI 数据中心也能如此——那些芯片似乎每隔几年就得更换。也许我们最终会剩下几家谦逊的科技巨头，以及为所有人的 AI 需求提供更廉价的算力。但我确实略微担心：随着这一轮债务周期推进得越来越快，经济宿醉会比以往更难受，因为靠债务驱动的资本开支狂潮往往收场很糟。

turns.en: So I don't want to be too negative about it, because journalists like me were always overly shrill about these things, but I definitely think there are no reasons to be fearful yet, but there are definitely reasons to be wary.
turns.zh: 所以我不想太悲观——像我这样的记者总对这类事情过于大惊小怪——我确实认为还没到该害怕的地步，但有理由保持警惕。

turns.en: The story of bonds, which you go through in the book, features a really remarkable cast of characters. We've talked about Alexander Hamilton and Jay Cook, but there's also Nathan Rothschild, Michael Milken, Bill Gross, many others.
turns.zh: 你在书里讲的债券故事，人物群像极为精彩。我们聊过 Alexander Hamilton 和 Jay Cooke，但也有 Nathan Rothschild、Michael Milken、Bill Gross 等等很多人。

turns.en: Which of these people do you think is the most underappreciated or had the most meaningful impact on the bond market? Yeah, that's the correct question.
turns.zh: 你觉得这些人里谁最被低估，或者对债券市场的影响最有分量？是的，这是个恰到好处的问题。

turns.en: It might be a bit like choosing your favorite child. I would say Jay Cook, because Jay Cook and Coe obviously went bankrupt in 1973, and maybe because this fall was so, and this was an era of no limited liability, like he personally went bankrupt.
turns.zh: 这可能有点像挑最爱的孩子。我会说 Jay Cooke，因为 Jay Cooke 公司显然在 1873 年破产了，也许因为这次跌落太惨——那是有限责任还很有限的年代——他个人彻底破产了。

turns.en: It went from probably America's richest man to bankruptcy courts. Because of that, I think his legacy isn't quite as appreciated. He was a financier that bankrolled the North's victory in the Civil War.
turns.zh: 他从大概美国最富有的人，一路沦到破产法庭。正因如此，我觉得他的遗产并不那么为人称道。他是一位为北方在内战中取胜提供了资金的金融家。

turns.en: I think without Jay Cook, history could have, in theory, looked differently. I'm not an expert on the Civil War and the military battles and stuff like that.
turns.zh: 我认为，没有 Jay Cooke，历史本可能在理论上走向不同。我不是内战和军事战役的专家。

turns.en: But it's very clear in the South, they saw Jay Cook and the financing he raised for the North as enormously consequential. And Ulysses S. Grant as well also thanked Jay Cook for basically being the man who saved the Union.
turns.zh: 但很清楚的是，南方视 Jay Cooke 及其为北方筹得的资金为举足轻重。Ulysses S. Grant 也感谢过 Jay Cooke，称他基本上就是拯救了联邦的那个人。

turns.en: Though that story does come from Jay Cook, and as you might have guessed, he was not a man of immense humbleness. So he might have embellished what Grant told him.
turns.zh: 只是这个故事出自 Jay Cooke 本人之口，而你大概能猜到，他可不是个多么谦逊的人，所以也许他把 Grant 对他说的话添油加醋了一番。

turns.en: But I mean, in our present day, Michael Milken, he's controversial because he got involved in the insider trading dragnet of the 1980s. He never went to a prison for that.
turns.zh: 但说到我们当下，Michael Milken 是有争议的，因为他卷入了 1980 年代的内幕交易大扫荡。他并没有为此坐过牢。

turns.en: There was other stuff, essentially, that he got dragged by the SEC and DOJ for Drexel Burnham Land. But the bank that he turned from not really an also ran, as it was always even near that, powerhouse for a period, died soon afterwards.
turns.zh: 还有别的事情——基本上他和 Drexel Burnham Lambert 被美国证券交易委员会（SEC）和司法部（DOJ）盯上追查。那家他一手从名不见经传、从没挨到第一梯队的公司，一度做成了巨头，只是不久后就倒了。

turns.en: And maybe because of all those legal controversies, I don't think he gets his due in that also junk box. So Mike Milken is the father of junk bomb, the modern junk bomb market.
turns.zh: 也许正是因为那些法律争议，我不认为他在“垃圾债”（junk bond）这块得到了应有的评价。Michael Milken 是现代高收益债、也就是“垃圾债”市场的开创者。

turns.en: And that just because of his name has negative connotations. But really, I think his genuinely brilliant insight that was transformative for America and frankly, the world today is that he felt a lot of companies weren't able to issue bonds because they were badly rated.
turns.zh: 只因为这个名字带负面含义。但我觉得，他那个真正天才的、对美国乃至今天全世界都具有变革性的洞见在于：他觉得很多公司因为评级低而发不出债券。

turns.en: And that was unfair. So they paid way too much and made more money from investors to lend to these kind of non-investment grade companies that were pejoratively called junk, but then to lend to IBM on general electric and so on.
turns.zh: 这不公平。所以它们向投资人付得太多，而投资人借给这些所谓“非投资级”——被讥称为“垃圾”——的公司本该拿得更多，反而去借给 IBM、通用电气（General Electric）这样的公司。

turns.en: And he turned that into not just an idea or a trading strategy, but he created a market out of that. And that is a stunning achievement. There are so many other examples of great financiers and investors and bankers and analysts have had these kind of insights that have taken it to like very far, but not to the point where they've genuinely created an industry.
turns.zh: 他把这不仅仅变成一个想法或一套交易策略，而是从里面造出了一个市场。这是了不起的成就。有太多伟大的金融家、投资人、银行家、分析师都有过类似的洞见，把它推得很远，却没到真正开创一个产业的程度。

turns.en: And yes, junk bonds were for a large part, at least in the 80s, mostly used by corporate raiders and there's lots of controversy around that, but I still think today's leverage finance market, high yield, leverage loans, private credit, CLOs, people like me sometimes write mean things about it because dumb stuff happens there, of course, but it is an incredibly valuable innovation.
turns.zh: 是的，垃圾债很大程度上，至少在 80 年代，主要被公司狙击手（corporate raiders）所用，围绕它有太多争议。但我仍然认为，今天的杠杆融资市场——高收益债（high yield）、杠杆贷款（leveraged loans）、私募信贷（private credit）、担保贷款凭证（CLO）——像我这样的人有时会对它说些刻薄话，因为那里当然会发生蠢事，但它是一项极具价值的创新。

turns.en: And that doesn't mean that there won't be silly things that happen in leverage funds and that are happening today, but that is actually a hugely valuable thing that it allows a lot of companies that can't go to the banks or can't go to the investment grade bond market that they can still access capital.
turns.zh: 这并不意味着杠杆融资基金不会出蠢事、如今没在出蠢事。它其实是极有价值的：它让很多既上不了银行、又进不了投资级债券市场的公司，依然能拿到资本。

turns.en: And that's incredibly powerful and is a large reason why America is still today, despite all its challenges over the years, the world's hyperpower.
turns.zh: 这是无比强大的，也是美国尽管多年来挑战重重、至今仍是世界超级大国的一个重要原因。

turns.en: And today, now in Europe, as much as they sometimes like to be snooty about American financialism and all that, in practice, Europeans would kill to have the leverage finance ecosystem that Mike Milken helped birth.
turns.zh: 如今在欧洲，尽管他们有时摆架子看不上美国式金融主义，但论实际，欧洲人会为拥有 Michael Milken 帮助催生的这套杠杆融资生态而拼命。

turns.en: So I think he's one of those people that maybe, I mean, certainly in American financial circles, he gets his due, but more broadly speaking, as somebody who's been quite consequential character for a U.S. in 20th century, maybe he doesn't quite get his due, though he's been obviously spending a lot of money on his reputation in recent years.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得他正是那样一个人——至少在 American 金融圈里，他得到了应有的评价。但更广泛地说，作为 20 世纪对美国相当有分量的人物，也许他还没得到应有的敬重——尽管近年来他显然花了不少钱来经营自己的名声。

turns.en: So maybe like, yeah, I just think he's a really interesting character and person and probably does not get the respect he should get, maybe, because of all these other quite often bad things that have happened around then as well.
turns.zh: 所以也许，是的，我只是觉得他是一个非常有趣的人物，大概没能得到他应得的尊重，也许是因为围绕那个时代发生的很多别的坏事。

turns.en: Robin, I want to harken back briefly to the example of Poyer, if for no other reason than it might be one of the more extreme examples from the book, from history, of just how problematic informationally symmetry can be in markets in general.
turns.zh: Robin，我想短暂回到 Poyais 的例子，哪怕只因为那或许是书里、历史上最极端的例子之一——关于信息不对称（information asymmetry）在市场里能有多糟。

turns.en: And you spend some time, and I think rightly so, addressing how informationally symmetries in the bond market, just the broad sort of collection and dissemination of critical information, be it just the basics of some of these issuers and subsequently ratings on many of their credits, many of their bonds became, like, how critical in hindsight was that in the modernization of bond markets, and what is their impact as we see them and
turns.zh: 你花了不少篇幅——我觉得很有必要——去讲债券市场里的信息不对称，也就是对关键信息的搜集与传播，无论是这些发行人的基本状况，还是后来对它们信用、对它们债券的评级。事后回看，这对债券市场的现代化有多关键？在我们今天如何使用这些信息、这些评级上，又产生了什么影响？

turns.en: use these bits of information, these ratings today? No, it was huge. And this was actually, I wrote in my chapter, of course, on the birth of the rating agencies, that I wasn't necessarily planning on writing, but I just felt it was essential because it also allowed me to examine this exact theme of informational asymmetries or a portion of information.
turns.zh: 我们如何对待这些评级？嗯，那是巨大的。事实上，我在写评级机构诞生那一章时——那是我本来不一定打算写的——只是觉得必不可少，因为它也让我得以探讨信息不对称、信息不全这个主题。

turns.en: And some of it just obviously reflects the error that there was no internet in the 19th century. But generally speaking, I think we sometimes forget how slowly information percolated in general.
turns.zh: 其中有些显然反映的是年代限制——19 世纪没有互联网。但总的来说，我觉得我们有时会忘记，信息的传播在过去有多缓慢。

turns.en: You know, the reason why Greg McGregor was able to do his scam for so long was because people didn't really understand. I mean, Latin America for most people in Britain and Europe might as well have been the moon or Mars.
turns.zh: Gregor MacGregor 的骗局之所以能持续那么久，就是因为人们其实不了解。对英国和欧洲的大多数人来说，拉丁美洲简直和月球、火星一样遥远。

turns.en: You know, it was incredibly, you just heard stories about it. You didn't even read that many stories about it. There were only a few maps and they were, you know, incredibly rudimentary in the financial markets.
turns.zh: 你只是听人说的那些故事，甚至没读过多少关于它的报道。当时地图很少，而且非常粗糙——在金融市场里也是如此。

turns.en: Like, better information, or information in general, but ideally better information. Information helps investors feel more confident. It is the reason why we mandate so much disclosure for public lists of companies that if you're going to sell your shares to the public, you should need to give the public more information.
turns.zh: 更好的信息，或者说信息本身——最好是更好的信息——能让投资人更有信心。这就是为什么我们强制要求上市公司披露那么多信息：你要是向公众卖股票，就该向公众提供更多资料。

turns.en: The bond market obviously has slightly different rules, but generally speaking, transparency is a good thing as well. Like I said, the Venetians, the English, they started revealing some rudimentary financial detail.
turns.zh: 债券市场的规则显然略有不同，但总的来说，透明也是好事。正如我说的，威尼斯人、英国人，都开始披露一些基础的财政细节。

turns.en: But still, for the longest time, essentially, you lent money to your local city-state or your province or a Dutch burger or, you know, the UK if you were a British investor.
turns.zh: 但在很长一段时间里，本质上你只是把钱借给你本地的城邦、你的行省、某个荷兰市民，或者——如果你是英国投资人——借给英国。

turns.en: Over time, as the bond market became more confusing, more international, you had Prussia and Italy and France and Russia ishing bonds. You kind of substituted the bank's reputation.
turns.zh: 随着债券市场变得更复杂、更国际化——普鲁士、意大利、法国、俄罗斯都在发债——你转而依靠银行的声誉。

turns.en: So the bank that chose to underwrote the bond was kind of putting their name on the line and would quite often buy a big chunk of the bonds themselves for their own, on their own account.
turns.zh: 于是承销这笔债券的那家银行，等于是把自己的招牌押上去，常常还会替自己买下其中很大一部分。

turns.en: They'd quite often, if it was a company, they'd go on the board, like Jay Cook would sit on boards. And that was how you kind of knew that, oh, well, Jay Cook sits on this board and he's famous because he helped bankroll the north.
turns.zh: 如果是公司，他们常常还会进董事会——像 Jay Cooke 就会在好几家董事会任职。就这样，你多少能判断：哦，Jay Cooke 在这家公司的董事会里，他很有名，因为他帮北方筹过资。

turns.en: Ergo, you know, this must be a good investment. And for a long time, that kind of worked. I mean, a great case of this is, for example, Nathan Meyer Rothschild and his descendants did not really get that involved in the Latin American bond craze because they felt there were bad credits.
turns.zh: 那么，这一定是笔好投资。很长一段时间里，这一套确实管用。一个绝佳的例子是，Nathan Mayer Rothschild 及其后人——他们其实没怎么参与拉丁美洲那阵债券热潮，因为他们觉得那是劣质信用，

turns.en: They wouldn't work out and they didn't want to peril their besmirch, their name, by underwriting all these dodgy bonds. And Ergo is one of the reasons why they managed to grow, whilst other big banking houses and families suffered quite a nightmare in the 1825 crash.
turns.zh: 不会有好结果，他们不愿为了承销这些可疑债券而玷污自己的名声。这也是为什么他们能够持续发展，而其他那些大银行家族在 1825 年的崩盘里吃尽了苦头。

turns.en: But of course, the Jay Cook example showed that trusting a bank's reputation only takes you so far. And if you can't trust Jay Cook himself, and he went bankrupt, well, then you're on your own.
turns.zh: 但当然，Jay Cooke 的例子说明：只靠信任一家银行的声誉，能带你走那么远而已。如果你连 Jay Cooke 本人都信不过——而他破产了——那你就只能靠自己了。

turns.en: And in this void, that's where we saw the first credit rating agency start to emerge in some of their protein form. And there's no coincidence that they emerged in the United States and people, banks in the UK started sometimes grading their borrows or prospective borrows by numbers or letters.
turns.zh: 正是在这片空白之中，我们看到了最早的信用评级机构（credit rating agency）以某种雏形开始出现。它们在美国兴起绝非偶然。在英国，银行、投资人有时会用数字或字母给借款人或潜在借款人打分。

turns.en: But credit rating agency as an industry that analyzed bonds and gave that information to the public emerged in the US because the US had embraced bond markets better than everybody.
turns.zh: 但作为一个行业——分析债券、把这些信息公之于众的信用评级机构——之所以在美国兴起，是因为美国比任何国家都更充分地拥抱了债券市场。

turns.en: The information was way worse because the country was so big that if you were an investor from Massachusetts, you knew nothing about borrows in South Carolina.
turns.zh: 那里的信息糟糕得多，因为国家太大：你要是马萨诸塞州的投资人，对南卡罗来纳州的借款人一无所知。

turns.en: That was a different country practically. So the rating agencies stepped in there. They didn't always do a great job. But despite all the criticism they get over the years and decades and centuries, broadly speaking, credit rating agencies, at least by the major ones, have proven to be not awful, not as awful as some people might actually think.
turns.zh: 那实际上就是另一个国家了。于是评级机构趁虚而入。它们做得并不总是很好，但尽管几十上百年里饱受批评，总的来说，至少几家主要的评级机构并没有那么糟糕——不像有些人以为的那么糟。

turns.en: And that's why they are this weird thing that cropped up in the 19th century that's still so huge and integral to the fixed income universe today, to a fascinating degree.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么它们成了那种 19 世纪冒出来、到今天却依然庞大、依然是固定收益世界不可或缺的怪东西——迷人得很。

turns.en: One central theme in the book is that the bond market has increasingly replaced banks as the dominant source of credit. When did that shift start taking place or take form?
turns.zh: 书里有一个中心主题：债券市场日益取代银行，成为信贷的主导来源。这一转变是什么时候开始成形、或成型的？

turns.en: And what do you think are the implications of that? This was the genesis for the book in many respects. Annoying that BIS data I looked at actually is imperfect.
turns.zh: 你觉得它的影响是什么？从很多方面说，这正是本书的缘起。国际清算银行（BIS）那份数据其实很不完善，让人有点恼火——

turns.en: It doesn't include a lot of Chinese bank assets. So knowing that we don't know exactly. But it probably happened at some point in the 2010s.
turns.zh: 它没把大量中国资产计入。所以既然我们无从确切得知，但这大概发生在 2010 年代的某个时候。

turns.en: But it's been a long time coming. And I think really the big changes, again, started in the United States, where the bond market probably has for a very long time been bigger than the banking system.
turns.zh: 不过这转变酝酿已久。我认为真正的大变革同样始于美国——在美国，债券市场可能很久以来就比银行体系更大了。

turns.en: The banking system in the US has always been extremely hemmed in by regulation or a complete lack of regulation, the wildcat banking era, for example, and a lack of a federal reserve, a central bank, meant that banking crisis is basically this obliterated part of the banking system every seven years, almost for a period.
turns.zh: 美国的银行体系一直要么被监管层层束缚，要么则完全缺乏监管——比如自由银行（wildcat banking）时代——缺乏美联储、缺乏央行，意味着金融危机差不多每七年就把银行体系的一部分抹掉一次，有一段时间几乎如此。

turns.en: But if you think about after World War II, the US was dominant. It was the center of the financial universe. And you started seeing finance becoming more creative, especially after the Nixon shocking 1971, that de-anchored the dollar from gold.
turns.zh: 但想想二战之后，美国一家独大，是金融宇宙的中心。你开始看到金融变得越来越有创造力，尤其是 1971 年的“尼克松冲击”（Nixon shock）把美元和黄金脱钩之后。

turns.en: Credit could finally be free because it wasn't somehow weighed down by needing to be pegged to something. And currencies were just something that traded between countries and they should float.
turns.zh: 信贷终于可以“自由”了，因为它不再需要被盯住某个东西。货币从此就是国与国之间交易的、理应自由浮动的东西。

turns.en: And you can see this kind of Cambrian explosion of innovation in the financial system in Europe as well, but particularly so in the US, where you see your first Mike Milken transform something that was in existence, the word non-investment grade securities before he was around, but he turned it into a legitimate market that you could issue non-investment grade bonds, which would have been almost unthinkable before Mike Milken.
turns.zh: 你能看到金融体系里一场“寒武纪大爆发”式的创新，在欧洲也有，但在美国尤其明显：Michael Milken 把原本就存在的东西——在他之前就有“非投资级证券”（non-investment grade securities）这个词——变成了一个合法的市场，让你能发行非投资级债券，这在 Milken 之前几乎不可想象。

turns.en: And that kind of actually meant that a lot of assets and loans that normally would have gone to the banking system migrated out of the banking system.
turns.zh: 这实际上意味着，很多原本会流向银行体系的资产和贷款，从银行体系里迁了出来。

turns.en: Then you have Louis Ranier at Solomon Brothers, another just incredible character, right? And it's also hugely transformative and probably also wrongly maligned because he's the father of securitization.
turns.zh: 然后是 Solomon Brothers 的 Lewis Ranieri，又一个了不起的人物，对吧。他也极具变革性，而且或许也被不公地贬低了，因为他是资产证券化（securitization）之父。

turns.en: And because of what happened in 2008, that name has been for a long time mud, and I think that's unfair. I think what he did again was actually genuinely fascinating, important and valuable, which is why we still have mortgage-backed securities today.
turns.zh: 因为 2008 年发生的事，这个名字长久以来被泼了脏水，我觉得这不公平。他所做的其实又迷人、又重要、又有价值——正因如此，我们今天还有抵押贷款支持证券（mortgage-backed securities）。

turns.en: They are still a massive part of the American financial system and the global financial system. But it meant that a lot of mortgages, credit card loans, I mean basically anything that is a cash stream can be turned into a bond.
turns.zh: 它们如今依然是美国金融体系、全球金融体系里庞大的一部分。但这也意味着，很多抵押贷款、信用卡贷款——我是说，基本上一切能带来现金流的东西——都能被变成一笔债券。

turns.en: So that was the magic of securitization and why you saw, especially in the United States, the financial system started shifting dramatically from being always not enormously bank-dominated to being bought 20% as banks, and the rest is the capital markets, essentially, in some form or fashion.
turns.zh: 这就是资产证券化的魔力。也是为什么，尤其在美国，金融体系开始从“从来都不是特别银行主导”急剧转变——大约两成归银行，其余的、以某种形式，都归资本市场。

turns.en: Europe has been slower. Europe has always had a bigger, more established banking network, but Europe is also changing as well. And we saw this particularly after the financial crisis, which I always argue that it's not really, we think it was a banking crisis, but that's reductive.
turns.zh: 欧洲慢一些。欧洲一直有更大、更根深蒂固的银行网络，但欧洲也在变。我们在金融危机后尤其看到这一点——我总是说，我们以为那是场银行危机，但那是一种简化。

turns.en: It was always certainly essentially not complete. It was as much a bond market crisis, I'd say, but really after the crisis, banks were the locus of all populist anger, understandably so.
turns.zh: 它当然是、本质上并非完全的银行危机——我说它同样是一场债券市场危机。危机之后，银行成了所有民粹怒火的靶子，这可以理解。

turns.en: So we basically stopped on lots of regulation on the banking system. That again, just kind of accelerated and squeezed risks out of banks into the markets, and particularly at the bond market.
turns.zh: 于是我们基本上给银行体系套上了重重监管。这又一次把风险从银行挤压、赶进了市场，尤其是债券市场。

turns.en: And that is a good thing, but it does have consequences that flow from that. And I mean, there are so many interesting ones. One is just central banking that we used to think QE was unorthodox monetary pulse, we called it.
turns.zh: 这是好事，但它有随之而来的种种后果。其中有很多有意思的，其一就是央行——我们过去以为量化宽松（QE）是非常规货币政策，是这么叫它的。

turns.en: My argument in the book is that QE is a natural, inescapable, and necessary evolution of monetary policy in a financial system where the bond market extends more credit than the banking system, that the central banks have set up the banks and set overnight rates.
turns.zh: 我在书里的论点是：在债券市场发放的信贷多于银行体系的金融体系里，QE 是货币政策一种自然、不可避免、必要的演进——央行设立银行、设定隔夜利率，

turns.en: That makes perfect sense if you just have a bank dominated financial system, but in something like what we have today, central banks have to care about the long end of the bond market as well.
turns.zh: 那在银行主导的金融体系里完全说得通。但在我们今天的这种体系里，央行也必须关心债券市场的长端。

turns.en: It's inevitable. I think financial regulation that we have, it's a great thing that banks are safer, but those risks don't disappear. I mean, it's not an original metaphor, it's almost a cliché at this point, but if you think of risk as energy, you can't really alter it, you can just change its form or move it from one place to the next.
turns.zh: 这是必然的。我认为我们所实行的金融监管：银行更安全是好事，但那些风险不会消失。这不是什么原创比喻，如今几乎成了老生常谈——但如果你把风险想象成能量，你无法真正消灭它，只能改变它的形式、或把它从一个地方挪到另一个地方。

turns.en: We move risk out of the banking system, which is good because they do all sorts of other important things, control payment systems. We don't want banks to fall apart at the slightest crisis, but that risk hasn't disappeared.
turns.zh: 我们把风险从银行体系里搬了出来，这是好事，因为银行还做着一堆其他重要的事——掌控支付系统。我们不希望银行在 slightest 危机面前就土崩瓦解。但那风险并没有消失。

turns.en: This is migrating the bond market, and that's a better place for it. It's usually far less leveraged, but it's harder to see because the bond market is the original decentralized finance.
turns.zh: 它正迁移进债券市场，而那是它更好的去处。债券市场通常杠杆率低得多，但它更难被看清——因为债券市场才是最早的“去中心化金融”。

turns.en: When people talk about DeFi today, I was like, dude, we've had this for a millennia. The bond market is DeFi. That is one of its ultimate strengths, but it's also one of its ultimate weaknesses.
turns.zh: 当人们今天谈论 DeFi（去中心化金融）时，我心里就想：伙计，这玩意儿我们都用了一千年了。债券市场就是 DeFi。那是它最终极的优势之一，但也是它最终极的弱点之一。

turns.en: The Fed, New York Fed, together all the big banks in one boardroom at Maiden Lane and say, guys, we're going to do X or Y, you couldn't gather every bond investor in America, even to the big mutual fund groups in one room.
turns.zh: 美联储、纽约联储，把各大银行召集在 Maiden Lane 的一间董事会议室里说：诸位，我们要做 X 或 Y——但你没法把全美国每一个债券投资人都聚到一起，就算那些大型共同基金集团也聚不进一间屋子。

turns.en: You couldn't gather them in one stadium, and that just makes it harder to know where the weaknesses are and not just where the weaknesses are, but how those weaknesses will flow into other weak links and how things can cascade.
turns.zh: 你连一座体育场都装不下他们。这就让弄清弱点在哪里变得更难——不只是弱点在哪里，还有这些弱点如何传导到其他薄弱环节、事情如何级联失控。

turns.en: It also requires them less keen on this, but I think it's inevitable, almost like a spray and pray approach by central banks. One of the reasons why, when there's a big crisis, I don't really know what's breaking.
turns.zh: 这也让央行更不太想较真，但我认为这是必然——几乎是央行“广撒网、碰运气”（spray and pray）的做法。原因之一是，当大危机来临时，我并不真知道是什么在崩坏。

turns.en: They just know it's bad. So it's just tempting, well, we're going to buy a ton of treasuries. We're even going to start buying corporate bonds as they did in March 2020.
turns.zh: 他们只知道情况很糟。于是很容易就想：好吧，我们大买国债，甚至在 2020 年 3 月像他们那样开始买公司债。

turns.en: We're going to do a limited repo. We are just going to throw money at the problem until the acute piece goes away. I just think that's inevitable, unavoidable, but I wish more people were aware of it, and we thought about ways that we cannot escape financial crises.
turns.zh: 我们做一点限回购（limited repo），我们就朝着问题撒钱，直到最急迫的那阵过去。我觉得这是必然、无法避免的，只是我希望更多人意识到这一点，希望我们明白：我们无法逃脱金融危机。

turns.en: The crazy thing is that I don't think the optimal number of financial crisis is zero. Then we'd have to control risk and risk-taking so violently that it would kill any sub-dynamism in the system, but we can certainly make those crises less apocalyptic and make sure that they don't spiral completely out of control and always require spraying money at it.
turns.zh: 疯狂的是，我不认为金融危机的最佳次数是零。若真那样，我们就得极其强力地管控风险和冒险，那会扼杀体系里的任何活力。但我们当然可以让这些危机不那么末日化，确保它们不至于彻底失控、永远都得靠撒钱来救。

turns.en: So I would like to see a greater appreciation, maybe more regulatory attention put on the non-bank part of the financial system because there's very little done there, and it just seems inevitable for me at least that the nature of financial crises has already evolved quite dramatically over the past 20 years, and will continue to evolve and be primarily pay themselves out in markets and credit markets rather than the banking system.
turns.zh: 所以我希望人们更重视金融体系的非银行部分，也许监管也该多关注那里——因为那方面做得太少。至少在我看来，这不可避免：金融危机的性质在过去 20 年已经发生了巨大演变，并将继续演变，主要在市场和信贷市场里自我消化，而非在银行体系里。

turns.en: Rob, in one of the recurring characters or at least prototypes throughout the book are quote, unquote, bond vigilantes, in my mind they almost feel like they're like the high lender of the story of bonds.
turns.zh: Robin，书里反复出现的一个角色——或者至少是一个原型——是所谓的“债券义警”（bond vigilantes）。在我脑子里，它们几乎像是债券故事里的大反派。

turns.en: They never die. They take on new identities as the years go on. Can you define what you mean by, and just what the market in general means when we talk about bond vigilantes, and are there bond vigilantes as one might say in the room with us now?
turns.zh: 它们永不消亡，随着年头更替不断换上新的身份。你能定义一下你所指的、以及市场一般所说的“债券义警”吗？此时此刻，房间里是不是也有债券义警？

turns.en: Who are they? And what are they worried about in 2026? Well, yes, but let me name it, we are the bond vigilantes. The bond vigilantes are us, right?
turns.zh: 它们是谁？它们在 2026 年担心什么？嗯，是的，但让我点名一下：我们就是债券义警。债券义警就是我们，对吧？

turns.en: We are usually some form of respect either directly buying the bonds of our governments or indirectly through mutual funds or pension plans and savings.
turns.zh: 我们通常是直接或间接购买本国债券的人——要么直接买政府债券，要么通过共同基金、养老金和储蓄间接持有。

turns.en: It's a phenomenal term that I frankly, my relationship with it has waxed and waned over the years. It was first coined by Ed Yardeni in the 80s to describe this kind of phenomenon of the bond market beating up usually poorer countries that were corrupt, had bad economic and financial policies, and the bond market would punish them by refusing to lend to them.
turns.zh: 这是个绝妙的词，坦白说我和它的关系这些年忽冷忽热。它最早是 Ed Jardeni 在 80 年代造出来的，用来描述一种现象：债券市场狠狠教训那些通常较穷、腐败、经济财政政策糟糕的国家——债券市场通过拒绝借给它们来惩罚它们。

turns.en: And it's both incredibly useful and incredibly misleading because it does evoke this kind of image of people going around beating up, you know, posses of people going around beating up bad companies and countries for doing the wrong thing, and that in reality, the bond vigilantes, the bond market, the power it has really is just, it has the power to slightly increase your cost of borrowing or in extremists and not lend to you.
turns.zh: 这个说法既极其有用，又极其误导。因为它唤起一种画面：一群人四处奔走、结成“义警队”去殴打那些做错事的公司和国家。可现实中，债券义警——也就是债券市场——真正的威力，只是让你的借贷成本稍微上升一点，或者极端情况下干脆不借给你。

turns.en: And that's not a superpower in theory, but of course in practice, in a world that runs on credit and a financial system that runs globally on credit, that is an awesome power as well.
turns.zh: 理论上这算不上超能力，但当然，在一个靠信贷运转、一个全球金融体系都靠信贷运转的世界里，这也是一种可怕的威力。

turns.en: So I both think the bond vigilantes metaphor is unhelpful because it sort of simplifies through an absurd degree, a very complex nuance reality, but it is also quite handy and useful and evocative and not entirely wrong in describing why the bond market matters to normies that I think should love it as much as I do, even though it's a hard sell at times.
turns.zh: 所以我既觉得“债券义警”这个比喻没什么帮助，因为它把一个极其复杂、微妙到荒谬程度的现实简化了；又觉得它确实挺顺手、有用、形象，也不全错——它解释了债券市场为什么对“普通人”（normies）重要，我多希望他们也能像我一样热爱它，尽管有时候这真的很难推销。

turns.en: But you know, what's been so interesting is seeing that the bond vigilantes go from targeting the perennial targets like Argentina or Greece to the United States of America, and that's the new one, I think.
turns.zh: 不过，最耐人寻味的是看到债券义警从那些“老对手”——阿根廷、希腊——转向美利坚合众国。我觉得这才是新鲜事。

turns.en: Robin, there are so many parts of the book that we didn't have time to talk about, but before we wrap things up, maybe we can just talk briefly about the end of the book where you discuss rising global debt levels.
turns.zh: Robin，书里太多部分我们没时间聊了。在收尾之前，我们能不能简短聊聊书的结尾——你谈到了全球债务水平的攀升。

turns.en: How concerned are you about that issue and the sustainability of sovereign debt levels today? Yes, it's the $150 trillion question now, I'd say.
turns.zh: 你对这个问题有多担心？今天主权债务水平的可持续性如何？是的，现在这就是那个 150 万亿美元的问题了，我会这么说。

turns.en: I'd say I'm more concerned than I was, but probably less concerned than most people in the world, if that makes sense. And that I feel we have been fretting about this for a very long time, I mean for 30, 40 years, and these things can change quite quickly.
turns.zh: 我想说我比以前更担心了，但大概比世界上大多数人更不担心——如果这话讲得通的话。我觉得我们为这事已经焦虑了很久很久，我是说三十四年了，而情况可以变化得相当快。

turns.en: The national debt clock in New York, that was built in the late 70s, early 80s, I think. And people were worried about America's debts then, but literally by the 90s, the Treasury stopped auctioning 30-year bonds because there were such big budget surpluses, people genuinely thought America would basically be debt-free, and why should they issue 30-year treasuries when locking that high borrowing costs for American taxpayers when the US was paying
turns.zh: 纽约那个国债钟（national debt clock），是 70 年代末、80 年代初建的，我想。那时候人们就在担心美国的债务。可到了 90 年代，财政部干脆停发了 30 年期债券——因为财政盈余太大，人们真的以为美国基本上能无债一身轻。既然美国在一路还清债务，又何必发行 30 年期国债、把那么高的借贷成本锁在美国纳税人身上呢？

turns.en: down all its debts? So things can change quite quickly. And broadly speaking, we don't lend money to margins. We're lending money to each other, essentially.
turns.zh: 所以事情可以变化得很快。总的来说，我们并不是借给火星，我们本质上是在互相借贷。

turns.en: And there are fragilities sometimes involved with that. The Trump administration going around being mean to foreigners that still buy trillions of dollars worth of treasuries can kind of inject extra fragility, perhaps.
turns.zh: 而这里面有时带着种种脆弱。特朗普政府到处对那些仍在购买数万亿美元国债的外国人生硬刁难，或许会注入额外的脆弱性。

turns.en: But I actually think that especially for big developed countries, and above all for the United States, there is a far greater capacity to carry debt than people think.
turns.zh: 但我确实认为，尤其对大型发达经济体、尤其是美国来说，承受债务的能力远大于人们所想的。

turns.en: Japan is a great example. There are nuances there in that its net debt levels are not as horrific as its nominal debt-to-GDP ratio might imply.
turns.zh: 日本就是个好例子。那里有一些细微之处——它的净债务水平，并不像它名义上的债务与 GDP 之比所暗示的那么可怕。

turns.en: But what I worry about, and the reason why I say I'm not worried, I'm more worried now than I used to be, is that for me, the solution as it were, the solution is usually multiple ones, has always been letting inflation run a little bit hot for a bit longer.
turns.zh: 但我担心的，也是为什么我说我现在比以前更担心的原因——对我来说，解决问题的办法通常是多种并用的，而历来就是：让通胀稍微热一点、多持续一阵子。

turns.en: I mean, in 2022 when inflation went up, look, I understand this seems almost heartless to say and inflation can hurt obviously poorer households far more than richer ones.
turns.zh: 我是说，2022 年通胀上来的那会儿——我知道这话听起来近乎冷酷，通胀显然对较穷的家庭伤害远大于较富的家庭，

turns.en: So it's inherently sort of very unequal impact. But the biggest reduction in global debt ever in history was 2022, because nominal GDP was growing so quickly with high inflation.
turns.zh: 所以它的影响天生就很不平等。但史上全球债务最大幅度的一次下降就发生在 2022 年，因为高通胀让名义 GDP 增长得飞快。

turns.en: And I thought the best thing would have been to let that run hot for a few years. And actually then a lot of things would look a lot less stretched.
turns.zh: 我当时觉得最好的做法是让这“热度”多延续几年，那样很多东西看起来就不会那么紧绷了。

turns.en: And that's not painless, definitely there are no easy choices here. But compared to some of the alternatives, I think that would have been possibly a better thing.
turns.zh: 这并非无痛，这里绝对没有轻松的选择。但相比一些其他选项，我觉得那也许是更好的做法。

turns.en: What I radically underestimated was our inability to tolerate faster inflation. We were talking about 60s or 70s or 80s level inflation. We were talking high single digits in most developed countries.
turns.zh: 我严重低估的，是我们无法容忍更快的通胀。我们聊的不是六、七、八十年代那种通胀水平，在多数发达经济体我们说的是个位数高段。

turns.en: And that's no fun. I hated it as well. But I thought it would have been better now, given that seems politically unpalatable. I do worry about like what are other ways around it.
turns.zh: 那也不好受，我也讨厌它。但我觉得那样做对现在会更好。鉴于这在政治上难以下咽，我确实担心：那还有什么别的出路？

turns.en: So now my assumption has been for a few years now that we think debt crises, like we think like Argentina or Greece, you know, your default restructuring move on.
turns.zh: 所以这几年我的预设一直是：我们想象中的那种债务危机——像阿根廷、希腊那样，违约、重组、重新出发——

turns.en: I don't think that happens in a country like the United States. I can literally print dollars. And we always kind of have this visceral sense of like an acute debt crisis, runaway bond yields, treasury selling off as foreign as flee or people panic and so on and that forces a change.
turns.zh: 我不认为它会发生在美国这样的国家。我基本上能印美元。我们总有一种本能的想象：一场急性债务危机，债券收益率失控、国债被抛售，外资逃离或人们恐慌，从而迫使某种改变。

turns.en: I don't think it's going to happen. I think the US is maybe in the early stages of what I'd call a chronic debt crisis. And it's just very slow, very gradual.
turns.zh: 我不认为那会发生。我觉得美国也许正处于我所说的“慢性债务危机”的早期阶段。它非常缓慢、非常渐进。

turns.en: But basically it starts snowballing that the US has to borrow so much, its debt stock is so big. As a refinance, all those treasuries issued at 1, 2, 3% at 3, 4, 5, 6%.
turns.zh: 但基本上它开始滚雪球：美国要借这么多，债务存量这么大，当它以 3%、4%、5%、6% 的利率去再融资（refinance）那些当初以 1%、2%、3% 发行的国债时——

turns.en: So even if the budget was balanced, the US would be locking in higher and higher, basically cost interest payments. And of course, sadly, the budget is far from balanced today.
turns.zh: 所以即便预算平衡，美国也在把越来越高的利息成本锁定下来。当然，令人遗憾的是，如今的预算远非平衡。

turns.en: But then you can start seeing things snowball that the cost of just simply servicing the debt is growing and growing and growing. So like countries have to start running to the set on top of it.
turns.zh: 于是你会开始看到它滚雪球：仅仅偿还债务的成本就一路攀升，国家不得不开始把盈余也拿去填这个窟窿。

turns.en: And you've seen this actually, one of the best examples is Canada. So Canada went on a bit on the debt spree in the, I think, 60s and 70s, but into the 80s.
turns.zh: 你其实已经看到过这种事。最好的例子之一是加拿大。加拿大在——我想是六、七十年代，一直延续到八十年代——有过一阵举债狂潮。

turns.en: And they didn't really get on top of inflation as much as other countries. But so they have to start jacking up interest rates, interest rates went higher, the provinces had borrowed too much money, Ottawa had borrowed too much money, so interest rates started going up.
turns.zh: 而他们不像别的国家那样把通胀控制住。所以他们不得不开始拉高利率，利率一路走高。各省份借了太多钱，渥太华（联邦）也借了太多钱，于是利率开始攀升。

turns.en: And their debt servicing costs, like just how much it cost, the economy as a whole to service government debts, went from 2%, 3% of GDP to 5% and then really started to snowball and hit almost 10% in the peak in the mid 90s.
turns.zh: 而他们的偿债成本——也就是整个经济体为偿还政府债务要付出的代价——从 GDP 的 2%、3% 升到 5%，然后真的开始滚雪球，到 90 年代中期峰值时几乎逼近 10%。

turns.en: And then they had to go full service and said, this is ridiculous. So much of our budget is getting eaten up by servicing debts. This cannot continue.
turns.zh: 然后他们不得不全面整顿，说：这太荒唐了，我们预算里有这么多都被偿债吃掉了，这不能继续下去。

turns.en: And for me, it's just, if you eyeball it, you can see that around 5% interest payments to GDP seems to be one of those areas where countries normally turn around and fix things like the UK in the 80s, all things start snowballing in a sort of dramatic way.
turns.zh: 而对我来说，你只要瞄一眼就能看到：利息支出大约达到 GDP 的 5%，似乎就是那种国家通常会掉头、着手修补的临界点——比如 80 年代的英国——各种事情开始以剧烈的方式滚起雪球。

turns.en: And the US is still far from that. The US is, I think, is around this year, kind of a 3.6% of GDP. I think it's 3.5%, 3.6% of GDP is going to debt servicing costs.
turns.zh: 而美国离那还远。美国，我想大概今年，偿债成本大约占 GDP 的 3.5%、3.6%。

turns.en: And that is not great. And it is definitely going higher, but it still is another decade before it hits kind of 5%-ish. So I just think the real chronic debt crisis in America, and frankly, look, I don't want to, I mean, you asked about the globe and I worry about that, but we can have debt crisis in France and Dambi and places like that.
turns.zh: 这算不上好，而且肯定还在往上走，但还要再过一个十年才可能触及 5% 上下。所以我认为美国真正的慢性债务危机——坦白说，我不想，我是说你问的是全球，我担心那个——但我们可以在法国、意大利等地发生债务危机。

turns.en: And it can be painful, but they're not of global consequence, but everything that happens in the US matters to everybody else to a far greater degree.
turns.zh: 那可能很痛，但它们不至于有全球性的后果。而在美国发生的一切，对其他所有人来说，其分量都要大得多。

turns.en: This debt crisis doesn't play out in hyperinflation, doesn't play out in runaway bond yields. It plays out as debt eroding America's financial health and being able to spend less on other stuff it wants to spend money on, whether that's defense.
turns.zh: 这场债务危机不会以恶性通胀收场，也不会以失控的债券收益率收场。它表现为债务一点点侵蚀美国的财政健康，让它在本想花钱的地方——比如国防——能花的钱越来越少。

turns.en: There's lots of focus on the fact that interest payments now consume more of the federal budget than defense does. But infrastructure, healthcare, education, all sorts of other things that the US maybe would like to spend on the arm, it is less able to as that kind of interest bill swells and swells and swells and it's a chronic crisis rather than an acute one.
turns.zh: 眼下很多关注聚焦在：利息支出如今在联邦预算里占的份额，已经超过了国防。但基础设施、医疗、教育，以及美国本可能想投入的种种——随着那笔利息账单越滚越大，美国在这些方面能做的就越来越少。这是一场慢性危机，而非急性危机。

turns.en: Maybe it'll become an acute one. I just think that kind of classic acute debt crisis that people envisage might never occur in the US since it's so unique and certainly won't play out any time soon.
turns.zh: 也许它最终会变成急性危机。我只是认为，那种人们设想的、经典的急性债务危机，在美国也许永远不会发生，因为它实在太特殊；而且短期内肯定不会有。

turns.en: I think we are now just, this was a very long answer to a question that obviously is we think a lot about now, but my view is that this is a chronic debt crisis that will be far slower to play out than most people appreciate, but it can still end up being quite painful nonetheless.
turns.zh: 我想我们现在只是——对一个我们显然都在反复琢磨的问题，我给了一个很长的回答。但我的看法是：这是一场慢性债务危机，它会比多数人意识到的慢得多地展开，但它最终仍可能相当痛苦。

turns.en: Yeah, and hopefully we'll figure out how to fix that chronic crisis before it becomes acute. Yeah, no. I mean, you can budget services. You remember those things?
turns.zh: 是的，希望我们能在慢性危机变成急性危机之前，想出办法解决它。是啊，我是说，我们可以精简预算开支嘛。这东西你还记得吧？

turns.en: Right. Bring back the 1990s. Yeah, unlimited spending isn't sustainable forever. No. But on that note, I want to thank you so much for joining us today.
turns.zh: 没错，把 90 年代带回来。是啊，无限开支不可能永远持续。不会的。但话说到这儿，我要衷心感谢你今天加入我们。我真的很喜欢这本书，和你聊得也非常愉快。

turns.en: I really enjoyed the book and it's been wonderful talking to you. Thanks for having me on. I really appreciated it and lots of great questions and I could talk for days about their stuff.
